title: Given a list of intervals each with a start and an end, merge all overlapping intervals and return the list of non-overlapping intervals that cover the same ranges. Solve it with the sort-then-sweep merge-intervals pattern and demonstrate with a complete banking mini-project.

s1_definition.oneliner: Sort by start, sweep left to right, extend the current interval on overlap using max-end, and start a new interval on a gap.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Merge intervals** – combine overlapping or touching intervals into a minimal non-overlapping set covering the same ranges.
- **Sort by start** – ensures overlap detection is local; only compare with the most recently merged interval.
- **Max-end rule** – when merging, take Math.max(currentEnd, nextEnd) so a fully contained interval does not shrink the current one.
- **Gap detection** – when the next start exceeds the current end, close the current interval and start a new one.
- **Final flush** – always add the last current interval after the loop to avoid the off-by-one bug.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, Rajesh consolidates account-lock windows. Some locks overlap when multiple operations run concurrently. He sorts locks by start time and sweeps once, merging overlapping windows into the true locked periods that the regulator needs for audit reports.

sections.s6_takeaway:
The merge intervals problem sorts intervals by start and sweeps once, extending the current interval when the next overlaps and starting a new one when there is a gap. Sorting is the enabling move: once intervals are in start order, overlap detection becomes local because any overlap must involve the most recently merged interval.

The two correctness traps are the max-end rule and the final flush. When merging, take Math.max of the current end and the next end, because the next interval might be fully contained and the current end must not shrink. After the loop, always add the last current interval to the result, because it is only closed by a gap that may never come.

At National Bank of India, the account-lock service merges overlapping lock windows to give the regulator the actual total time an account was under any exclusive lock. Sorting the windows by start and sweeping once collapses all overlaps into the minimal set of distinct locked periods, keeping audit-report generation fast even for busy accounts.

This is the foundational problem of the interval-problems family. Insert Interval, Interval Intersection, Meeting Rooms, and free-gap computation all build on this sort-and-sweep skeleton. A senior engineer recognises it as a reusable pattern and knows to use `Instant.compareTo` for real timestamps and `BigDecimal.compareTo` for monetary ranges.

Remember one sentence: sort by start, sweep with max-end to handle containment, flush the final interval, and you have the minimal merged set.

---

keyPoints: Sort by start makes overlap detection local: only compare with the most recently merged interval.
Max-end rule: Math.max(currentEnd, nextEnd) prevents shrinking when the next interval is fully contained.
Final flush: always add the last current interval after the loop to avoid the off-by-one bug.
Use <= for the overlap test when touching intervals should merge, < when they should stay separate.
Time is O(n log n) for the sort plus O(n) for the sweep; space is O(n) for the output.
This sort-and-sweep is the foundation of all interval problems: insert, intersect, meeting rooms, free gaps.
